Getting started

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

This article shows the three things most users do first: simulate a price scenario, see how one household responds to it, and run the full agent-based model. For how the model works, see vignette("model-description").

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("phalacrocorax-gaimardi/depmicrosimr")

Load the package. Its scenario table sD is the base scenario used throughout.

library(depmicrosimr)
head(sD[, c("parameter", "value", "unit")])
#>            parameter    value  unit
#> 1   dep_introduction 2026.500  <NA>
#> 2   tou_introduction 2021.000  <NA>
#> 3       old_vat_rate    0.135  <NA>
#> 4       new_vat_rate    0.090  <NA>
#> 5 post_2030_vat_rate    0.135  <NA>
#> 6   dynamic_cap_2026    0.500 €/kWh

1. Simulate retail prices

set_prices() simulates one wholesale price path from 2026 onwards (observed prices before that) and turns it into hourly flat, ToU and dynamic tariffs. It draws random numbers, so every call gives a different path.

set.seed(1)
prices_scen <- set_prices(sD)
head(prices_scen)

2. How one household responds

get_flex() takes a table with columns datetime, price and load (the household’s natural load, in kWh per hour) and returns the optimal shifted load load_opt. The parameters are the inflexible fraction phi, the behavioural cost weights gamma and eta, and the load-shift timescale tau in hours.

library(dplyr)

demand <- prices_scen %>%
  filter(tariff_plan == "dynamic", lubridate::year(datetime) == 2026) %>%
  inner_join(load_profiles_generalised %>% select(datetime, lp1)) %>%
  mutate(load = 4200 * lp1) %>%          # a household using 4,200 kWh a year
  select(datetime, price, load)

response <- get_flex(demand, phi = 0.4, gamma = 5, eta = 0.3, tau = 24)

# share of annual energy that was moved to another hour
100 * sum(abs(response$load_opt - response$load)) / (2 * sum(response$load))

Plot one winter week of natural against shifted load:

library(ggplot2)
week <- response %>% filter(lubridate::yday(datetime) %in% 32:38)

ggplot(week, aes(datetime)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = load, colour = "natural")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = load_opt, colour = "shifted")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(natural = "grey50", shifted = "orange")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "kWh per hour", colour = NULL)

Larger gamma makes shifting costlier, so load moves less. Larger tau lets the household move load further in time before it is penalised. Increasing phi makes more of the load inflexible.

3. Run the agent-based model

runABM() runs one or more independent simulations. Each builds its own price path, social network and agent population, then steps forward in two-month intervals from January 2019. Dynamic tariffs are introduced in mid-2026, so the run has to extend past that date to see any dynamic adoption.

set.seed(42)
res <- runABM(
  sD,
  Nrun            = 2,
  simulation_end  = 2030,
  behavioural_model = "prospect",   # "full" also counts the behavioural penalties
  use_parallel    = FALSE           # TRUE uses several cores (macOS/Linux/Windows)
)

names(res)          # "abm" "scenario" "system"
dim(res$abm)

Start with Nrun = 1 and a short horizon: every sampled household solves several optimisation problems at each step.

res$abm has one row per household, per date and per simulation. To see adoption over time, count households by tariff plan:

adoption <- res$abm %>%
  count(simulation, date, tariff_plan) %>%
  group_by(simulation, date) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

ggplot(adoption, aes(date, share, colour = tariff_plan, linetype = factor(simulation))) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "share of households", colour = "tariff plan", linetype = "run")

Before smart meters are installed, households are on flat or the old tou_old day/night tariff. tou appears as smart meters are installed, and dynamic after mid-2026.

Things to know

  • Reproducibility. The model is stochastic at every level. set.seed() fixes a single-process run (use_parallel = FALSE). Parallel runs are not reproducible with R’s default random number generator.
  • Price paths are not returned. runABM() returns the household states but not the price path that each run used.
  • Choosing a behavioural model. "prospect" and "full" are the current models. "full" is the default in runABM(); see vignette("model-description"), section 7.
  • Scenarios. sD is the base scenario. Other scenarios are sheets in inst/ext_data/scenario_parameters.xlsx and can be read with readxl::read_xlsx() into a data frame with the same columns as sD.
